articles.title: Utah library confirms LGBTQ 'Pride' book for its 'smallest patrons' is kept easily accessible
articles.summary: The Provo City Library confirmed to Fox News Digital it includes "Pride is Love" and other LGBTQ board books in its collection, saying they are shelved among 2,500 titles.
articles.body: A Utah public library confirmed to Fox News Digital that an LGBTQ-themed children's book highlighted by a conservative outlet is part of its collection for its "smallest patrons" and is intentionally kept "central and easily accessible," while pushing back on claims that the book was on display. "I can confirm that the library does own a copy of ‘Pride Is Love’ along with the other small board books that were pictured in the post you referenced," Carla Z. Gordon, director of library services at Provo City Library, told Fox News Digital in a statement Tuesday. "They are not on display," Gordon added. "They are shelved in bins that contain over 2,500 other board books (any that are currently checked in). The post describes them as being 'central and easily accessible,' which is very true. These are books for our smallest patrons and we make them easy to find." OREGON SCHOOL COUNSELOR FACES BACKLASH OVER 'CHOSEN FAMILY' BOOK FOR YOUTHS On Monday, The Cougar Chronicle, which identifies itself as providing "independent conservative news and opinion at BYU," posted a photo of the book "Pride Is Love," with a caption that read, "EXCLUSIVE: The Provo City Library children's section is promoting radical gender theory, critical race theory, and other progressive propaganda to Provo's children." The thread also included photos of other LGBTQ children's books, including titles such as "Pride Puppy!," "It's a They!," "My Two Dads and Me," and another called, "My Moms Love Me." TRANSGENDER DOLLS TO BE AVAILABLE FOR MINNESOTA SCHOOLCHILDREN AS YOUNG AS 4 UNDER WALZ-BACKED PROGRAM: REPORT The Amazon page for the book, "Pride is Love," says it is intended for babies through age three and is about a girl and her two dads as they prepare to march in a Pride parade. Similarly, "My Two Dads and Me," is also intended for babies through age three and shows the day-to-day of LGBTQ fathers and their children through everyday routines, from breakfast and trips to the park, to bath time and bedtime. WASHINGTON MOTHER PULLS CHILDREN FROM SCHOOL AFTER PRIDE LESSON SHOWN IN MUSIC CLASS WITHOUT NOTICE In her statement, Gordon referenced a portion of the library’s website she said has been created to help parents select materials that match their family values. Gordon also highlighted the library’s Selection Policy, which is to "collect, organize, and make easily available to the people of the community materials which will help them in the pursuit of education, information, and the creative use of leisure time." "Within the limits of space and budget, the collection offers patrons materials in a choice of format, treatment, and level of difficulty," she added. "In this way, most individual library needs can be met and service provided to individuals of all ages." PORTLAND PARENT FIGHTS CHILD'S ELEMENTARY SCHOOL OVER 'FINAL STRAW' OF ADDING TRANS-INCLUSIVE FLAG "These particular books are not currently on display, but we do have many displays throughout the library that try to highlight books available," Gordon said. "We sometimes use holidays, observances, visiting authors, popular topics, and completely random themes all in attempt to promote our collections." "As mentioned in the Selection Policy, we do try to represent differing perspectives on many topics," she added. "Gender, sexuality, and race are all topics that have a variety of perspectives, so we do own books representing those differing voices."  "We do receive complaints from parents and community members about materials in the collection. The process is outlined in the policy referenced above," Gordon added. "When we receive these concerns, we review the materials and follow the process to either retain, move, or discard items." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, appeared to express concern about the situation in a Monday post on X, sharing the thread from The Cougar Chronicle and writing, "Come on, Provo You’re better than this."

articles.title: Firms scramble for battery power in Spain and Portugal
articles.summary: After last year's massive power failure Spanish and Portuguese firms are buying battery back ups.
articles.body:
On the 28 April last year, Portugal and Spain went dark for several hours.

A massive power failure caused widespread chaos . People dug out lanterns and old radios, and companies scrambled to save what production they could.

The Spanish meat processing firm Fribin, in Binéfar, in the north eastern province of Aragon, was midway through its morning shift when the sudden shutdown brought production lines to a halt.

For Andrés Altabás, Fribin's technology and systems director, it was a nightmarish situation.

Emergency systems didn't have the capacity for continued operation. "Refrigeration was prioritised but all the lines had to be stopped," he adds.

Many tonnes of meat in the processing stage had to be discarded. "There were losses of hundreds of thousands of euros," says Altabás.

The bosses at Fribin realised they had to rethink their back up plans.

It was a big undertaking as the company's energy needs are "quite large", amounting to more than 25 gigawatt-hours a year, most of it for refrigeration.

The business had been considering investing in a battery back-up system for years, but it had been judged too expensive.

"And then came the blackout, and all of that together catalysed the investment," Altabás tells the BBC.

The first purchase of a five megawatt-hour module was made in June 2025, and a second module with the same storage capacity was ordered in early June 2026, both amounting to a total investment of around €1.5m (£1.3m; $1.7m), funded in part by the European Union's Next Generation funds.

Firms across Europe have been switching to electricity from fossil fuels for their industrial needs, encouraged by subsidies from EU funds.

While that is helping bring down emissions of climate-warming gases, it has also made firms more vulnerable to power cuts.

And in Spain and Portugal that threat was made painfully clear last year.

On both sides of the border, firms are looking for ways to avoid disruption.

"The industrial sector has been one of the first to look at storage systems, since it can't have its production drop off too abruptly," says Miguel Matias, founder of the Portuguese energy services company Self Energy, headquartered in the UK.

"A backup for a few hours, or even minutes, might guarantee that machines don't get damaged," he says.

And there have been more recent incidents to spur investment.

At the end of January, Storm Kristin toppled thousands of electricity and telecom poles across central Portugal, cutting power and communications to hundreds of thousands of people - some for weeks.

So, companies and other organisations have been taking action.

In Spain, battery storage capacity has risen almost sevenfold since last April, from about 28 MW before the blackout to 193MW in April 2026, according to the grid operator Red Eléctrica.

In December, the IDAE, Spain's Institute for the Diversification and Saving of Energy, awarded €827m in EU funds to 133 energy storage projects totalling 2,400MW. Around 80% of that is battery storage.

The new capacity will be close to 10 times the amount that Red Eléctrica currently registers on the Spanish grid.

It's all good news for battery suppliers.

"We are seeing not only an increase in demand, but also a clear evolution in customer requirements," says Alberto Bodegas, from battery storage company Sungrow.

Traditionally, commercial and industrial clients were looking for partial or full backup solutions, Bodegas says.

Today, Bodegas says customers are demanding more advanced capabilities, such as seamless backup, meaning the switch from grid to backup occurs instantaneously and without any noticeable interruption.

This is particularly critical for sensitive environments such as hospitals and data centres.

Delivery times are also crucial for buyers, currently under tight deadlines linked to EU funding programmes. Battery companies are being pressed to meet increasingly shorter delivery dates, Bodegas says.

Portugal's Vista Alegre, the oldest and largest porcelain maker in the Iberian country, decided to install energy storage systems in 2022, seizing the opportunity of abundant funds from the EU's Recovery and Resilience Plan.

"The blackout ultimately served, above all, to accelerate this process," Emília Encarnação of Vista Alegre explains. The company's facilities in the coastal city of Ílhavo, in the province of Aveiro, are now equipped with modules with around 2MWh of storage capacity.

"The blackout caused some irreparable losses, particularly at the plants operating on a continuous production basis, where sudden power interruptions have a direct impact on production processes," Encarnação recalls.

Advantages go beyond being able to respond to sudden shocks in the energy network. For example installing batteries also means the company can profit from selling energy into the general network.

At Primus Ceramics, located near the city of Aveiro, in central Portugal, a diesel generator saved the day during last year's blackout.

Their roller kilns - which transport materials through every production phase inside industrial ovens - are powered by electric motors.

During the power cut, the generator kept the products rolling, minimising the day's losses.

The experience accelerated the company's plan to make their production process more resilient, company CEO Paulo Almeida tells the BBC.

Primus already had two batteries installed in 2022 to back-up their energy supply and for selling electricity back to their energy company when market conditions were favourable.

By the end of this year Primus will have more than double its battery capacity, to store more energy from the factory's solar panels.

For Almeida, that would be reassuring after the stress of last year's blackout.

"We were at it until eight, nine at night, deciding whether we should stop, whether we should lower the furnace temperatures, or whether we'd take the risk and wait for the power to come back in time," he says.

The power did come back in time, but it was near miss for Primus.

articles.title: UK weather: Met Office warnings in force amid thunderstorm and flood risk
articles.summary: Torrential downpours will affect parts of England and Wales, delivering some of the wettest weather in several weeks
articles.body:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

The Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning covers a large swathe of England and Wales.

A band of showers and thunderstorms will push northwards during Wednesday morning with sunny spells following from the south.

However, further scattered downpours and storms will spring up during the afternoon.

As many as 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in some locations within just an hour, and it is even possible that 40-50mm (1.6-2in) could accumulate over a few hours.

However, due to the hit-and-miss nature of showers, some places will miss the rain and weather apps may struggle to get the detail of the forecast correct.

Where the rain does fall, flash flooding is a real concern. This will be especially problematic where the ground is hard after the prolonged dry spell, making it difficult for the water to soak in.

Difficult driving conditions are expected with the chance that some roads could be closed.

Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible.

Northern Ireland will also see some showers but these are likely to be less intense with less thunder.

Many parts of Scotland will remain dry with sunny spells, although some showers are likely in the south-west later.

Thursday will bring another zone of thunderstorms, again affecting mostly England and Wales.

The Met Office has issued a further yellow weather warning, valid from 06:00 until 22:00 BST.

Widespread rainfall totals of 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) are expected in the warning area within three hours, while some areas could see 50mm (2in) within the same timeframe.

There is a small chance that eastern-facing hills - exposed to easterly winds - could record 75mm (3in) during 12 hours, which would bring a significant flood risk.

The showers may eventually reach southern Scotland and Northern Ireland but are likely to weaken and become less intense as they drift northwards.

Wettest weather in weeks for parts of southern UK

Despite a period of unsettled weather last week, some southern parts of the UK have still seen barely any rain recently.

Brize Norton in Oxfordshire has recorded just 0.4mm of rain so far this August, less than 1% of what it would normally expect during the month as a whole.

Kew Gardens recorded no rain at all in July, and only 1.8mm so far this month.

It means the rain we are expecting this week is likely to far outstrip what has fallen recently in some areas.

What does 80 per cent chance of rain mean? Published 12 June

Why you may not see showers and thunderstorms on your weather app

Thunderstorms are often very hit-and-miss.

Some places can see flooding downpours while others, perhaps only a few miles away, avoid the heaviest rain and stay essentially dry.

Weather apps - including the BBC Weather app - can struggle in these scenarios.

Forecasters know that the conditions are ripe for storms to form, with warm humid air across the UK interacting with a zone of colder air pushing in from the west, higher in the atmosphere.

This generates low pressure and instability.

However, the computer weather models that drive weather apps will always struggle to pinpoint exactly where and when the biggest storms will spring up.

It is a bit like heating popcorn kernels in a pan.

You cannot know precisely which kernels will pop and in which order, while some kernels may not pop at all.

Some of the storms will also occur at night, which may mean they do not show up in the daily weather icons.

It is worth keeping an eye on the hourly weather symbols, as well as the percentage chances of rain, if you are making outdoor plans.

articles.title: Ball python 'Tippy' found caged in community garden as animal control seeks owner
articles.summary: Residents and garden staff told 311 they had seen someone leave the snake in a cage beside the garden beds.
articles.body:
A routine stream of found-pet notices in Boston took an unexpected turn when city officials shared an alert for a ball python, rather than the more familiar missing dog or cat.

A caged snake later identified as "Tippy" was discovered near the raised beds of a Dorchester community food garden, Boston.com reported .

Boston Animal Care and Control said the ball python turned up at about 6 p.m. at a community garden on Ellington Street in Dorchester, per the outlet. The animal arrived there under mysterious circumstances.

Before animal control arrived, residents and garden staff told 311 they had seen someone leave the snake in a cage beside the garden beds, a spokesperson told Boston.com.

An officer brought the reptile to the city's animal care facility in Roslindale, where officials said it was in good condition and getting proper care.

They posted a photo of the reptile to their Facebook account (@bostonanimal) in hopes of finding the owner.

Ball pythons are commonly kept as pets, but they are not native to Boston and are not animals that belong outdoors in the city. Leaving one outside can put the reptile at risk, especially if it is without the temperature control, food, and shelter it needs to stay healthy.

Commenters on Facebook were wary of foul play from an owner who might have abandoned multiple pets.

"MSPCA has five of these up for adoption," one commenter noted. "Hope there's no connection."

There was immediate concern for the animal, and some disregard for whoever left it.

"OMG poor snake," another Facebook user wrote. "The person is a snake, unbelievable."

Boston.com said Tippy is being kept at the city facility in Roslindale while Boston Animal Care and Control seeks information about the snake. Anyone with details is asked to contact the agency at 617-635-1800 or animalshelter@boston.gov.

Until then, the ball python remains in city care.

In general, if pet owners are unable to take care of a pet, leaving the animal outside should not be the next move.

Instead, contacting local shelters and care facilities that might be able to rehome and host the pets is a much better option for the animal and the local community.

articles.title: The backlash Pride faces from inside and outside the LGBT community
articles.summary: Big companies used to go out of their way to support Pride. Now, there's a nervousness in the air, Darren Milby writes
articles.body:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcoming… has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

Pride started as a protest, with Britain's first official Pride march in London in 1972. Homosexuality was illegal in the UK until 1967, and LGBT people lost jobs and housing because of their sexuality, while police forces frequently targeted the community with raids and surveillance that made everyday life precarious.

In Manchester, Pride started small in 1985. A bring‑and‑buy sale on Canal Street was organised to raise money to spruce up the rather drab-looking hospital ward treating those with HIV and Aids at the height of the epidemic.

Little did those early attendees realise how big Manchester Pride would become: a four-day, city centre extravaganza over the August bank holiday weekend, with colourful floats, loud music, and every inch of pavement filled with enthusiastic spectators dressed to the nines, streaked with rainbow face paint.

By 2019, the event had outgrown the city's famous Gay Village. That year's headline act, American superstar Ariana Grande, performed in a purpose-built stage in another part of Manchester - for a premium ticket price. It prompted criticism, and the organisers of Manchester Pride would later come under fire for ending funding for various charities (including an HIV charity, and a scheme that distributed free condoms).

The company behind Manchester Pride went into voluntary liquidation last year, owing more than £1m to suppliers and performers, including Nelly Furtado. Since its collapse, local businesses and charities have created a not-for-profit group - Manchester Village Pride - with the aim of organising a much cheaper festival more rooted in the community.

Carl Austin-Behan, who is helping to organise this year's scaled-back event, says he's been "frustrated for a number of years" by the direction of Manchester Pride. "When things were being taken out of the village, that was the first sign that things were going in the wrong direction… It should be about the community. We certainly don't need to be spending the amount of money that was spent on Manchester Pride."

And Manchester's problems aren't isolated. London Pride has faced criticism for feeling overly corporate and overcrowded; Brighton has struggled with the financial burden of staging large‑scale concerts and policing. Against that backdrop, smaller events like Crewe seem to be the direction many Prides are going in 2026.

But the political winds have also changed - with seemingly less corporate enthusiasm for diversity and inclusion initiatives.

Phil Douglas, organiser of Newcastle Pride, says: "There is a general nervousness from organisations and companies to be front and centre in their support. We see some wanting to still support us but not wanting their logo attached… they don't want the backlash which is right there ready in the online community. It's quite a complex time to navigate support for Prides as a whole."

A few years ago, you couldn't go on social media in June - known as "Pride month" - without seeing what felt like every corporate logo incorporating the Pride flag. Critics called it "rainbow‑washing", arguing that the displays of solidarity were more about marketing than meaningful action.

But now, according to Guardian analysis, the corporate presence has been waning. Last year, mentions of Pride on social media by the UK's 10 biggest listed or headquartered companies had fallen by 92% compared with 2023 - a drop that suggests brands are pulling back from overt LGBT messaging.

"There has been a general rowing back of corporate support for LGBT causes globally," says Paul Martin, chief executive of the LGBT Foundation charity. "We've seen that with politics changing in some countries and diversity and inclusion being seen as too woke… We don't get support from some quarters like we used to.

"And that has played out with Pride festivals as well. Corporate funding has been pulled back and that has caused a real challenge for Pride organisers to balance the books."

A survey by the pollster Ipsos found that the share of British adults who want companies and brands to promote LGBT rights dipped from 52% in 2021 to 44% this year.

In Liverpool, Merseyside Police did not take part in the city's Pride parade last year after legal advice warned that uniformed participation by a public body could breach rules on political impartiality.

This summer, firefighters and police again stayed away: Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said it was taking a "pragmatic approach" following a High Court ruling that found officers in the north‑east should not have been allowed to join a Pride event. West Midlands Ambulance Service also withdrew from Birmingham Pride on similar legal advice.

Back in May's local elections in England, Reform UK won power on 14 councils, adding to the 10 they already controlled. Last month, the party's leader, Nigel Farage, said he is "fine" with Pride events going ahead but did not want local authorities to promote them.

A few weeks after taking power in Durham last year, the town's new Reform administration removed a rainbow flag from the council headquarters. Councillors also withdrew their funding contribution of £2,500 for Durham Pride. In the Merseyside town of St Helens, meanwhile, the Reform council leader instructed officials to cease engagement with all aspects of Pride; the council also removed displays celebrating the festival from libraries.

Explaining the cuts to funding, Reform's Darren Grimes, deputy leader of Durham Council, says: "I feel that we've moved away from that laudable aim of gay equality. We achieved same-sex marriage and that was the final frontier."

Durham Pride organiser Mel Metcalf says taking the flag down made LGBT people in the community "feel unwelcome". The festival did still take place; organisers said it was their "biggest" year ever, after raising around £25,000 from individual donors and trade unions.

As well as Reform's approach, the new Conservative council leader in Enfield, north London, has said they will only fly certain flags outside Enfield Civic Centre - and the rainbow flag is not one of them.

Debate around trans rights is also fuelling the Pride culture war. Some gay and lesbian people who describe themselves as "gender critical" - and whose beliefs mean they're sceptical of some of the aims of the trans rights movement - say they feel sidelined by Pride; while some trans people say they no longer feel safe attending.

A lesbian woman who describes herself as gender critical, and did not want to be named, told me she no longer attends Pride because she thinks it has become dominated by a focus on trans issues.

Grimes, one of Reform's highest-profile gay members, argues that Pride has moved away from its focus on gay equality and become bound up with the wider gender identity debate: "You've slain the dragon in the pursuit of equality and now all you are left with is a few rambling sheep." He says that "public subsidy" for LGBT issues has become a "cash cow" that fuels "narratives of victimhood".

For some, the focus on trans rights is a reason to step back from Pride; for others, it underscores why events like Sparkle matter.

Sparkle is the UK's biggest transgender celebration. It takes place in late June in Manchester's Gay Village, a few months before the Pride weekend. This year's event had live music and comedy. Lauren, a transgender volunteer at the event, told me: "We've got a lot of stigma and hatred against us… You've got people trying to push us back into the dark and it does make it harder to live our lives."

Another transgender woman I spoke to, who was staying in a hotel in Manchester's Gay Village, said she wanted to be in the city for the event, but was wary of leaving the hotel because she felt unsafe.

Security has also become a central consideration, especially after the events of last month in Berlin, when 21-year-old Abdul Ballout drove a car into a crowd at the city's Pride festival, killing one woman and injuring 29 others. Guy Mathias, from the Security Commonwealth - a trade group for security firms - says he thinks many Pride organisers will review their plans following the Berlin attack.

"Smaller events generally would cost less individually, but they still need many of the same safety measures in place," he adds.

Others think that Pride festivals can create headaches for local residents. Andy Winter, a columnist for the Brighton Argus, attended Pride marches in the 1980s in his role as a Brighton councillor. He recalled in one piece how he was vilified by the press at the time for supporting a pro-LGBT council motion. But last year, he wrote that Brighton's Pride weekend comes with "alcohol and drug-fuelled excesses".

He wrote: "Even though I am not gay, Pride impacts on me. One of the parks I use is 'closed' for ten days... to allow largely straight performers to entertain those able to pay the large entry fee." He added: "The streets are littered with plastics and broken glass. I pity neighbours of the park and surrounding streets who see their driveways and gardens used as toilets."

I've been to dozens of Pride events over the years. Manchester has always been a must. When I was a teenager in Ulverston, Cumbria - a place where I was pretty certain I was the only gay in the village - Manchester always seemed like the bright lights, a land where you could be free and your true self.

This year I'll return again, excited to catch up with my friends and intrigued to see what the new community-focused Pride is all about.

But I suspect there'll be a slightly different mood in the air this year; an awareness that in some parts of the country, Pride has become controversial.

Younger LGBT people still say Pride matters. A 2024 YouGov survey of more than 500 LGBT Britons, aged 16 to 24, found that 90% say it is "very" or "fairly" important that Pride month still exists.

As a young man, I eventually left Ulverston to live in Manchester. But this summer I took a trip back to my old hometown for their Pride festival, a tradition still in its infancy.

The once-familiar cobbled streets looked so different to how I remembered them, lined with cheering locals clapping and filming on phones as a procession bedecked in rainbow flags swept past, led by a brass band playing upbeat gay anthems. It felt a world away from Manchester's famous pop stars and stages covered in corporate logos.

Matt had a similar reflection on returning to Crewe. "What really resonated with me and blew my mind was the fact that it was so family-centred. These small towns put on events that are for the community first and foremost."

As I looked around Ulverston, the national debates that have shaped Pride in recent years felt distant. I was distracted by the small things: people laughing, the spread of ages in attendance. It was the community my teenage self never would have imagined he'd see.

articles.title: Demetrius Fleming, 38, Found Hanging In Roanoke Rapids
articles.summary: An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that t...
articles.body:
An ongoing police investigation surrounds the death of a 38-year-old Black man found hanging last Friday morning. The police chief of the city reports that the cause of death is yet to be established.

The deceased man has been identified as Demetrius Eugene Fleming. Police Chief Lawrence Wiggins reported that police received a call just a little past 6:45 a.m. about a possible suicide case in the 1900 block of Roanoke Avenue. Fleming was discovered tied with a rope and declared dead at the scene.

According to Wiggins, Fleming was found dead when emergency personnel arrived at the house. Halifax County EMS and the Roanoke Rapids Fire Department were part of the effort. No information has been provided on the type of ligature used.

"We're treating this as an open, equivocal death investigation," Wiggins reported. This means that the cause of death is being investigated without making assumptions about whether it was a suicide, homicide, or accident. Wiggins stated that it would be premature to conclude and that the evidence would determine the cause of death.

At the afternoon press conference, Wiggins said that "anything is on the table" and detectives are exploring all angles of the case. When asked whether another person may be involved, he said everything is under consideration.

An autopsy is being carried out. According to Wiggins, the autopsy will provide the possibility to establish any other injuries on Fleming. Information should be available by Monday; however, it was not available by Tuesday.

According to Wiggins, police are aware of the case's history. He expressed his condolences to the family of Demetrius Fleming and added that they are cooperating with investigators since Friday.

The recent death case follows a similar incident that happened a week ago. Wiggins referred to the Raleigh case, where police ruled the death a suicide, according to WITN.

Chief Rico Boyce of Raleigh Police reported on Aug. 17 that video surveillance footage, along with traffic cameras, showed the 32-year-old man walking alone to the tree carrying an electrical cord, and investigators found no indication of anyone else's involvement. Boyce added that the woman's mother informed investigators of the man's mental problems.

The death of the 32-year-old man became an occasion of fear, pain, and concern for the population, according to the statement made by the North Carolina NAACP and its Raleigh-Apex branch.

The reason why the Raleigh death case received so much attention is the connection of a Black man found hanging from a tree in the South with the history of racist lynchings. Demetrius Eugene Fleming was originally from Roanoke Rapids, was born in January 1988, and his relatives said he was a husband and father.

Persons with information are encouraged to contact Halifax County Crime Stoppers at 252-583-4444 or via the P3 Tips app.

articles.title: Canadian man dies after being struck by a plane at Montreal airport
articles.summary: An airport worker at Montreal-Trudeau International Airport died after being struck by a plane.
articles.body:
An airport worker was struck and killed by a plane pushing back from the gate at Montreal-Trudeau International Airport Monday night after he reportedly tripped and fell on the tarmac.

According to Pax News , the aircraft was a French Bee Airbus A350 bound for Paris. About 7:30 p.m., the man, later identified by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) as 39-year-old Oscar Robayo, was struck by the plane as it moved.

Radio-Canada spoke to a witness who said the man went under the plane and that people began screaming once they saw what was happening.

Robayo sustained what police described as "serious injuries" and was rushed to the hospital by emergency crews. He was later pronounced dead.

The IAM said Robayo was a ramp agent with Samsic Airport, a company that operates out of the airport providing passenger services and baggage handling. ADM Aéroports de Montréal, which operates the airport, issued a statement after the accident.

"The ADM Aéroports de Montréal team is deeply saddened by the loss of a member of the YUL airport community, an employee of Samsic, following an accident that occurred while carrying out their duties," the airport operator said.

The company added that assistance and support were being provided to employees and passengers who witnessed the accident. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada is investigating.

articles.title: Fake Bank Call Convinced Her to Open Her Safe. Police Say a Man Drove Off With $1.5 Million in Jewelry and Metals
articles.summary: A phone call from people posing as bank employees ended with a stranger driving into a Florida woman’s garage and leaving with approximately $1.5 million......
articles.body:
A phone call from people posing as bank employees ended with a stranger driving into a Florida woman's garage and leaving with approximately $1.5 million in jewelry and precious metals from her safe, according to police.

Treasure Island investigators say the scammers first convinced the older resident that her bank accounts and credit cards had been compromised. She wired approximately $280,000 before a bank employee recognized a second attempted transfer as suspicious and stopped it.

Police say the callers then changed tactics. They warned the woman that employees at her own bank could come to her home armed and steal her valuables, then offered a supposed way to protect them.

The six-month investigation has resulted in the arrests of James Arthur Graves Graham Jr., 24, and Alnesha Bianca Handy, 35, while authorities continue trying to identify other participants and locate missing property, according to National Jeweler .

The Callers Posed as Chase and Bank of America Employees

Treasure Island police responded to the woman's home on Feb. 10 after a report involving fraud, grand theft and burglary. Police Chief John Barkley said the callers claimed to represent Chase and Bank of America. When an actual bank employee stopped another large wire transfer, the people on the phone did not end the conversation.

FOX 13 reported that the callers instead convinced the woman that employees at her own bank were involved in the supposed criminal activity. Police say the woman remained on the phone for more than four and a half hours as the callers used fear and urgency to keep her following instructions. She eventually told them that her valuables were stored in a safe in her garage.

The callers instructed the woman to open the safe and garage door and then go back inside the house so she would not see the person supposedly coming to secure her valuables. Police say a vehicle entered the garage and the door was closed. The person inside emptied the safe and drove away with approximately $1.5 million in jewelry and precious metals.

License Plate Cameras and Fingerprints Led Police to Graham

Neighborhood surveillance and Treasure Island's Flock license plate reader system helped investigators narrow a description of the vehicle to a specific truck.

Police identified Graham as the person they believe went to the residence. He reported the vehicle stolen the following day, and investigators later recovered it in the Fort Lauderdale area.

Authorities said surveillance footage and latent fingerprints provided additional evidence. Treasure Island detectives then worked with Tampa police to search Graham's apartment, where investigators say they found clothing consistent with what the person at the victim's home had been wearing. Graham was arrested on one count of first-degree grand theft and one count of second-degree burglary.

The Wire Transfer Led Investigators to Georgia

Detectives and investigators with the Sixth Judicial Circuit State Attorney's Office spent months following financial records and leads through Tampa, Miami, Fort Lauderdale, Georgia, California and Texas. Investigators eventually traced part of the victim's wire transfer to a Georgia account they say belonged to Handy.

The Tampa Bay Times reported that the account, held under the name Handy Helping Hands LLC, contained $114,000 from the original transfer when investigators traced it.

Treasure Island investigators traveled to Georgia and interviewed Handy before the DeKalb County Sheriff's Office arrested her. Police said she faces a grand theft charge.

Police Recovered More Than 83% of the Wire Money

Investigators recovered more than 83% of the approximately $280,000 transferred electronically and returned it to the victim. Barkley described that level of recovery as highly unusual because fraud proceeds are often moved rapidly through multiple accounts and can become difficult to trace. Authorities believe the case may involve a larger fraud network, and additional arrests remain possible.

A Bank Will Not Send Someone to Your Home to Protect Your Valuables

An unexpected caller claiming a bank account has been compromised should be independently verified before any money or property is moved. Treasure Island police advise customers to hang up and call their financial institution using a trusted number, such as the one printed on the back of a bank card.

Banks will not instruct customers to hand jewelry, cash, gold or other valuables to a courier for safekeeping. They also will not require customers to move money to another account simply to protect it from fraud.

If someone claims a courier or representative is already on the way to a home, do not open the door or surrender property. Contact local law enforcement and the financial institution independently.

Anyone who has already sent a wire should notify the originating bank immediately and ask whether the transfer can be recalled or frozen. Acting quickly matters because stolen funds can move through additional accounts within hours.

articles.title: ‘No Conclusions’ Made as Investigation into Flight Attendant Mom’s Death During Layover Continues, Police Say
articles.summary: “Detectives are conducting numerous interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video, and examining evidence,” police said after Jenny Lupton’s death
articles.body:
Jenny Lupton, a Southwest Airlines flight attendant, was found dead in Hawaii last week

Her family previously said authorities told them that she appeared to have fallen from the hotel's balcony, but an investigation into her death remains open

"At this time, no conclusions have been made regarding the manner of death," police said in a statement released on Monday, Aug. 24

The family of Jenny Lupton, the Southwest flight attendant found dead during a layover in Hawaii last week, continues to wait for answers about her death.

In a news release shared with PEOPLE on Monday, Aug. 24, the Honolulu Police Department said their unattended death investigation began in Waikiki on Thursday, Aug. 20.

"The HPD Homicide Detail is actively investigating the circumstances surrounding her death and is working closely with her family," police said. "At this time, no conclusions have been made regarding the manner of death."

"This is a thorough investigation that will take time," police continued. "Detectives are conducting numerous interviews, reviewing and recovering surveillance video, and examining evidence as part of the investigative process."

Lupton, 50, of Moore, Okla., worked as a flight attendant for 29 years and was also a mom of one, according to NBC affiliate KFOR and CBS affiliate KWTV .

Family members said the Honolulu Department of the Medical Examiner contacted them, stating that Lupton appeared to have fallen from a 24th-floor balcony at her Waikiki hotel.

Her sister Tresa told KWTV that a hotel employee found Lupton's body, while KFOR reported the discovery was made on Aug. 20.

When reached for comment by PEOPLE, a spokesperson for the medical examiner's office said that the cause and manner of Lupton's death have not been determined, noting that a final determination could take several months.

Lupton was in Hawaii for work but was planning to stay for several days before returning, according to her family.

Tresa recalled receiving a text from Lupton, who had just gotten a new tattoo, hours before she was found dead. "She just went out with one of her flight attendant friends, and they danced and had a good time," Tresa said during an interview with KWTV.

Hannah Lupton, Jenny's niece, told USA Today that the family does not believe their loved one died by suicide and "are worried that there is possible foul play involved."

In a statement shared with PEOPLE on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the Oklahoma Attorney General said their "office is in contact with Hawaii Attorney General Anne Lopez's office to help ensure a proper investigation into Jenny Lupton's death."

"We are also in contact with the Lupton family who deserve to have answers about this tragedy," the spokesperson added.

Southwest Airlines has also offered their "condolences and support" and says they "are engaged with local authorities as they investigate."

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

Honolulu Police have said that in order to preserve the integrity of the investigation, authorities "will limit the release of certain information while the investigation remains ongoing."

"On behalf of Jenny Lupton's family, we ask for patience as detectives conduct this investigation and respectfully request that the family's privacy be honored during this difficult time," the department added.

Additionally, authorities asked the public to refrain from sharing unverified information.

Meanwhile, a GoFundMe created for Lupton's family has raised over $11,000 as of Tuesday afternoon.

articles.title: US spy chief visits Russia for meetings, media reports
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reporte...
articles.body:
A C-17 Globemaster, believed to be carrying U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, lands near Riga, Latvia

WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, U.S. media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.

The ‌trip would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a ‌U.S. spy chief since Ratcliffe's predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Vladimir Putin in November 2021. About three months ​after that meeting, the Russian president launched Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.

CBS News and Axios reported the visit by Ratcliffe, U.S. President Donald Trump's CIA chief, who served as director of national intelligence in Trump's first term. The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what ‌the talks are expected to ⁠cover.

The CIA declined to comment. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov neither confirmed nor denied the report, telling Reuters President Vladimir Putin did not plan to ⁠have a meeting with Ratcliffe.

The U.S. last week asked Ukraine not to launch air strikes around Moscow, St. Petersburg, and some northern territories of Russia on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of this week ​because ​a plane carrying a senior U.S. official would ​be flying to the Russian capital, ‌said a source familiar with the matter.

The source declined to provide further information. The Financial Times first reported the U.S. message to Ukraine.

On Monday, the U.S. warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, a move aimed at stepping up economic pressure on Tehran to settle the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February.

The U.S. has no ‌ambassador to Russia, which maintains a close strategic partnership ​with Iran involving extensive military, economic and diplomatic ties.

Tehran ​supplied Moscow with drones for its ​war against Ukraine. In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused Russia of ‌supplying its version of those drones to ​Iran.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment ​reported by Reuters in April said that Russia has aided Iran with satellite imagery for use in targeting U.S. facilities in the Middle East.

Moscow denies providing such assistance ​and has said it ‌is ready to help resolve the U.S.-Iran conflict.

(Reporting by Daphne Psaledakis and Jonathan Landay; ​additional reporting by Vladimir Soldatkin in Moscow and Dan Flynn. Writing by ​Susan Heavey; editing by Chizu Nomiyama, Jekaterina Golubkova)

articles.title: 5-foot red-tailed boa constrictor found crossing rural road in Canada
articles.summary: Boas are known "escape artists," able to slip through surprisingly small gaps.
articles.body:
A 5-foot red-tailed boa constrictor found crossing a rural road in Ontario left everyone wondering where exactly it came from.

According to GuelphToday , Katherine Leonard, senior manager of community services at the Guelph Humane Society (GHS), said the humane society received a call from a resident after a large snake was seen on the road in Arthur near Eliza Street and Wells Street.

Before that call reached staff, another person in the community had already secured the animal in a large plastic container with duct tape, which was how it arrived at GHS.

The humane society does not usually handle animal control in the Arthur area, but staff still assisted in this special instance and pulled an old enclosure from storage, specifically saved for this type of situation.

During intake, Leonard said, the boa showed no immediate signs of illness or injury and appeared to be a fully grown adult measuring just over 5 feet long.

She added that the snake likely had not been outdoors for long and had "been previously cared for," indicating captivity rather than a wild animal encounter.

VCA Canada says red-tailed boas — also called common boas — are nonvenomous snakes from Central and South America that can grow to about 13 feet and often live 20 to 30 years. They are also strong climbers and require tall, secure enclosures in captivity.

Leonard said the humane society does occasionally receive surrendered ball pythons, but a snake of this size is unusual. "It's definitely one of the larger snakes we've seen here," she said.

Leonard noted that boas are known "escape artists," able to slip through surprisingly small gaps in doors, windows, and even ceiling tiles. She said another possible explanation is that the snake may have been dumped by someone who could no longer afford or handle its care.

Large snakes require space, specialized housing, and a long-term commitment — all of which can create serious challenges for owners and rescue organizations.

The snake is being held under the humane society's standard impound process. Leonard said the shelter will keep it through the required five-day period, after which it could be made available for adoption if no owner comes forward.

The shelter is also asking people who are missing a snake — or who know of one that has gone missing — to contact GHS.

Animals that can live for decades and require specialized habitats can quickly become difficult to care for when their needs are underestimated. When that happens, the consequences reach beyond a single household, affecting neighbors, rescuers, and the animal itself.

"It was crossing the road, so it's very fortunate it didn't succumb to any injuries," Leonard said. "Our hope with any animal is always to reunite it with its owner, but, in the event that it doesn't, that's what we're here for."

articles.title: Wood fire prompts evacuations in Riverside County
articles.summary: A fire in an incoporated area of Perris has prompted evacuation orders and warnings, authorities said.
articles.body:
A fire in Riverside County has prompted evacuation orders and warnings in the Inland Empire.

The Wood fire was burning near Orland and Roth roads in an unincorporated portion of Perris, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. It comes amid an extreme heat warning in many parts of Southern California, including in the valleys of San Bernardino and Riverside counties, for "dangerously hot conditions" with high temperatures up to 110 degrees.

The fire had burned about 60 acres as of 3 p.m. and is 0% contained, according to Cal Fire.

At 4:30 p.m., there were road closures on Salter Road at Fox Street, and at Juniper Road and Ida Leona Road.

Nearly 170 personnel have been deployed to respond to the fire, including three helicopters and 29 engines, Cal Fire said.

Officials issued evacuation orders for zones RVC-1060 and RVC-1059 shortly after 2 p.m., warning of "immediate threat to life." The evacuation area is bounded roughly by Orange Avenue to the north, Juniper Road to the west, Santa Rosa Mine Road and San Jacinto Avenue to the south and Old Elsinore Road to the east. An evacuation map can be found here .

Evacuees, and their pets, can go to the Perris Library at 163 E. San Jacinto Ave. for shelter and other resources, according to the order.

Officials also issued evacuation warnings for surrounding neighborhoods. The cause of the fire is under investigation, and it was not immediately known if there had been civilian injuries or structural damage.

Most of Harford Springs Reserve, a park featuring several hiking trails, is under an evacuation warning, according to the map. The northwestern part of Motte Rimrock Reserve, a biological field station on a rocky plateau managed by UC Riverside, also falls in an evacuation warning zone.

The blaze was reported just before 1 p.m. near the area of Rider Street and Dreamglo Lane, Cal Fire/Riverside County Fire Department posted on X. The fire was, at the time, burning at a "dangerous rate in medium grass and brush."

By 2:15 p.m., the agency said the fire was burning at a "moderate rate."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Instagram chief admits touting teen safety tool while omitting it was barely used
articles.summary: Adam Mosseri, who oversees Instagram at Meta, admitted in a California court on Tuesday that he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosi...
articles.body:
Adam Mosseri, who oversees Instagram at Meta, admitted in a California court on Tuesday that he touted newly launched safety tools for teens without disclosing low adoption rates from early testing several years ago.

With more than three billion users around the world, Meta is fending off accusations by a coalition of 29 US states that it deliberately designed its products to hook children and gather their data while misleading the public.

The trial entered its second week on Monday and is expected to last through late September.

A lawyer with the Colorado Attorney General's office, Jason Slothouber, questioned Mosseri about the low usage of the tools, known as Take a Break and Quiet Mode, which were launched in 2021 and 2023, respectively.

Other witnesses have testified over the past week that these tools weren't effective, though Mosseri pushed back on the idea that adoption remains low.

"This is one feature with a disappointingly low usage rate which since this time has significantly improved," Mosseri said.

On December 8, 2021, Mosseri testified at a Congressional hearing about the negative impacts of social media on young people. One day before, Meta published a blog post, authored by Mosseri, about rolling out new safety features for teens.

"Early test results show that once teens set the reminders, more than 90% of them keep them on," the blog post says.

However, that number referred to the number of people who kept it on after turning it on.

When asked if Meta disclosed its low adoption, which only reached 1 or 2 percent of the accounts, Mosseri admitted the company did not but said the safety features were later turned on by default in Teen Accounts, which have parental controls and launched in 2024.

However, Mosseri couldn't recall if Meta had ever disclosed the percentage of teen accounts that have parental controls turned on.

Mosseri will continue testifying on Wednesday. Founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg is also expected to testify, though it's unclear when.

Meta knew that its tools for protecting teenagers on Instagram were largely ineffective, other witnesses have testified.

Internal Meta documents shown to jurors on Tuesday said that Take a Break, which allows users to set reminders to stop scrolling, reached an adoption rate of 1.8 percent, while Quiet Mode, which silences late-night notifications, reached 8.7 percent.

Under questioning from state lawyers, Francesco Fogu, Meta's director of product design at Instagram, said Tuesday that he was not aware of the numbers, but conceded that the company "knew adoption rates would be lower" if those tools were not turned on by default.

Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who will decide the case using the jury's verdict as guidance, appeared stunned that Fogu was unaware of the internal data.

If Meta is convicted, US states will seek around $200 billion in penalties, and a court loss could force fundamental changes to its business model and send shockwaves through the industry.

Two former employees also testified that Take a Break and Quiet Mode were not effective.

"In my experience, Take a Break is a feature that's designed to fail," Arturo Bejar, a former Meta engineering director, testified last week.

George Volichenko, a data scientist who worked on safety features at Instagram in 2022 and 2023, said Monday that adoption rates for those features were "very low and disappointing" and just "a drop in the ocean."

He painted Meta's leadership as uninterested in meaningfully boosting their use.

Leadership did not approve turning on Quiet Mode by default for younger teens, which held down adoption because the setting was hard to find in the app, Volichenko said.

Switching the safety features on by default would have caused a "notable negative impact" on user engagement, he said.

Meta's business model revolves around selling advertising, and the company earns more when users spend more time on its apps.

articles.title: N.J. restaurant writes ‘happy wheelchair birthday’ on disabled customer’s dessert. Here’s what we know.
articles.summary: A birthday celebration ended with an unsettling message.
articles.body:
A birthday dinner at an upscale New Jersey restaurant took an unexpected turn when dessert arrived at the table with an insensitive message.

Antonia Sinibaldi , a Hudson County native who suffered a spinal injury in a car crash when she was 2 years old, spent her 29th birthday at Blu on the Hudson back in June with her friends and family.

When Sinibaldi's dessert arrived at the table, next to a lit candle was a message written in icing: "happy wheelchair birthday!"

"It took me by surprise," Sinibaldi, who has relied on a motorized wheelchair and ventilator for most of her life, told CBS News . "I shouldn't be reminded of something that I already know."

The Weehawken resident told CBS News she asked management for an explanation, but was unsatisfied with their response.

"He offered to send me more drinks, more drinks, more drinks," Sinibaldi told CBS News. "What good will that do?"

Sinibaldi declined comment at time of publishing. Messages left for Blu on the Hudson were not returned.

In a statement given to CBS News, Blu on the Hudson apologized for the incident.

"We at Blu on the Hudson are aware of the recent video circulating on social media, and we are deeply saddened by what occurred. We sincerely apologize to the guest and to everyone who was hurt or offended by this incident which took place on June 20, 2026. Treating every guest with dignity, respect, and care is fundamental to who we are as a company."

The statement went on to provide further context for the incident, noting Blu on the Hudson's staff uses tables and seat numbers to identify where dishes are delivered. "Wheelchair" was used as a reference for where the birthday dessert with a candle was to be delivered, but was not intended to be written on the plate.

"There was absolutely no malicious or disrespectful intent behind the notation," the statement read. "However, we fully understand how seeing that word written on a plate could be deeply hurtful and upsetting."

Blu on the Hudson also said in the statement it has since talked to the staff about the importance of proper ticketing and communication, in hopes of making sure an incident like this doesn't happen again. The restaurant said it also unsuccessfully attempted to reconnect with Sinibaldi to apologize further.

articles.title: Former news anchor pleads guilty to stabbing mother to death on Halloween
articles.summary: Angelynn Mock pleaded guilty to first-degree murder after allegedly believing her mother Anita Avers was the devil during the Halloween stabbing.
articles.body: A former Missouri television news anchor has admitted to fatally stabbing her mother on Halloween last year after apparently believing she was the devil, authorities said last week. Angelynn "Angie" Mock, 48, pleaded guilty to one count of first-degree murder in connection with the slaying of her mother, 80-year-old Anita Avers, on Oct. 31, 2025, the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office announced Friday. Under the terms of the plea, Mock faces life in prison with eligibility for parole after 25 years. FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING MOM AND BURNING BODY BECAUSE SHE ‘WANTED TO BE CREMATED’ Officers were called to the Wichita home Mock and Avers shared with Mock's stepfather around 7:50 a.m. on Oct. 31. When they arrived, Mock was found outside with cuts on her hands, according to the Wichita Police Department. Avers was taken to a hospital with multiple stab wounds, and later died. Mock made several statements indicating she believed her mother was the devil, according to a probable cause affidavit. She allegedly told authorities that she killed her mother to "save herself." Mock's stepfather told KAKE-TV that she had been diagnosed with mental illness and suffered from delusions and depression. FORMER TV ANCHOR ACCUSED OF KILLING HER MOTHER RULED INCOMPETENT, MURDER CASE PUT ON HOLD She previously worked as a news anchor and reporter for Fox 2 in St. Louis from 2011 to 2015, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to that, she worked as a morning anchor from 2007 to 2011 at KOKH-TV in Oklahoma City, the profile states. Mock held other reporting stints in Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska. articles.title: His Clinics Billed Medicaid More Than $36 Million in Six Months. A Plea Deal Calls for 15 Years in Prison
articles.summary: A Yuma doctor accused of using medical businesses he controlled to bill Arizona’s Medicaid program more than $36 million in a matter of months could... Read...
articles.body:
A Yuma doctor accused of using medical businesses he controlled to bill Arizona's Medicaid program more than $36 million in a matter of months could spend 15 years in prison under a proposed plea agreement filed in his criminal case.

Dr. Irfan Fazil, 54, founder of Bio Family Clinic, is accused of operating a racketeering enterprise that defrauded the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, known as AHCCCS, between July 2025 and May 2026.

Investigators say three AHCCCS-enrolled provider businesses controlled by Fazil and his spouse submitted more than $36 million in claims between July and December 2025 alone. The billing included tens of thousands of X-rays, more than 10,000 ultrasounds and more than 1,000 ECGs, according to KYMA .

The case took a major turn Aug. 25 when a plea agreement was filed calling for a 15-year prison sentence. Fazil has not yet formally entered the plea in court.

Patients Said They Never Received Some of the Services Billed

Court records reviewed by KYMA said the three provider entities' AHCCCS billing during the final six months of 2025 represented approximately 97% of their revenue for that year.

Investigators then compared the claims with information from patients. Multiple people said they never received services billed under their names, while some were outside Arizona or even outside the United States on dates when the records indicated treatment occurred.

The volume of diagnostic procedures also drew scrutiny, including the tens of thousands of X-rays, more than 10,000 ultrasounds and more than 1,000 ECGs cited in the probable-cause records.

The State Accused Him of Operating a Racketeering Enterprise

The case became part of Arizona's participation in the 2026 National Health Care Fraud Takedown. The Arizona Attorney General's Office said Fazil was charged with fraudulent schemes and artifices, illegal control of an enterprise, theft, conspiracy and drug-related felonies.

Prosecutors allege the enterprise operated from July 2025 through May 2026 and that Fazil conspired with another person to commit money laundering and theft. Bio Family Clinic was separately charged with fraudulent schemes and artifices.

The Proposed Deal Calls for 15 Years in Prison

Under the agreement filed Aug. 25, Fazil would receive a 15-year prison sentence for fraud, illegal control of an enterprise and theft, KYMA reported .

The proposed deal calls for conspiracy and possession of dangerous drugs charges to be dismissed. It would also require Fazil to give up his medical license and Drug Enforcement Administration registration. Another provision requires Fazil to provide authorities with passwords to his cellphones and laptops.

Fazil remains in the Yuma County Detention Center on a $50 million bond. Although the written agreement has been filed, KYMA reported Aug. 25 that he had not yet formally entered the plea before a judge.

His next court appearance is scheduled for Sept. 4. Until the plea is entered and accepted, the proposed 15-year disposition is not a final sentence.

Patients Can Report Medical Services They Never Received

Medical billing fraud can sometimes be detected by the people whose identities appear on claims, particularly when records show appointments, tests or procedures that never occurred.

The AHCCCS Office of Inspector General specifically identifies billing for services or supplies that were never provided, double billing, overbilling and incorrect coding as examples of potential provider fraud.

AHCCCS members who notice an unfamiliar service should compare the information with their own medical records and contact their health plan or provider for clarification. Dates when the patient was elsewhere, procedures the patient does not recognize or repeated services that never occurred should not simply be ignored.

Suspected provider fraud can be reported directly to AHCCCS OIG. The agency says anyone may make a report and that reports may be submitted anonymously.

We asked members of the BuzzFeed Community to share the dumbest thing someone they know said. Soooooo many people shared stupid things their husbands said, so, of course, I compiled the funniest ones. Enjoy:

1. "My favorite dumb thing my husband said (when I was pregnant) is that he thought babies don't wear diapers when they sleep. After laughing for a bit, I told him they still pee and poo in their sleep. He said he knew that, but he thought they wore a special nightgown or something in their sleep instead. articles.title: L.A. takes aim at phenibut, an unregulated 'gas station drug' that is growing in popularity
articles.summary: L.A. City Council hopes to regulate phenibut, a drug one councilmember says is widely available to children in gas stations and convenience stores.
articles.body:
Los Angeles is looking to regulate another "gas station drug" on commercial shelves.

In a unanimous vote Tuesday, the L.A. City Council instructed the City Attorney to draft new regulations for phenibut, a Cold War-era drug that is said to have been used by Soviet cosmonauts, but abused now as a central nervous system depressant.

Regulations will include restricting sales to people under 21, banning sales near schools and daycare centers and the creation of labels warning against its use, according to the motion .

The full council must vote again on ordinance language before the regulations become law.

"Phenibut is a powerful, unregulated substance that has been sold openly to kids at gas stations and convenience stores across our city, with no age restrictions and little warning of its risks. That ends now," said Councilmember Heather Hutt, who authored the motion.

Nina Paquette, a Marlborough High School senior, brought the existence of the drug and its dangers to Hutt's attention.

"The drug is often marketed directly to children, who are able to purchase it easily without any age restrictions," Hutt said. "Our young people are at extreme risk of developing a severe dependence on this easily accessible substance."

Phenibut is not federally regulated and cannot be legally sold as a dietary supplement. Despite that, Hutt said, it's easily available in L.A. convenience stores.

Paquette, a former intern for state Assemblymember John Harabedian (D-Pasadena), said phenibut pills are often marketed as "smart drugs" or "brain boosters" on social media.

"Teenagers can buy it at gas stations with no idea it can cause addiction, seizures, hallucinations, psychosis and coma," Paquette said.

In Russia, phenibut is a prescription drug used to treat anxiety, insomnia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and other ailments. It functions much like Valium or Xanax by depressing the central nervous system, and has been banned in several countries and Utah .

According to some studies , phenibut can be addictive and cause withdrawal symptoms. Studies looking into poison control reports found it can lead to trouble breathing , coma or death. Researchers warn that it is an up-and-coming drug that western medicine knows little about.

It's not the first time an unregulated gas station drug has come under fire in L.A.

The Southeast Asian plant kratom and its alternate powerful synthetic alkaloid 7-OH, another drug that escaped federal regulation for years and regularly sold in gas stations and smoke shops, was linked to six overdose deaths across L.A. County last year.

Kratom was temporarily deemed a scheduled substance by the FDA and has been pulled from shelves across California , according to Governor Gavin Newsom.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Texas nature center rebuilt after Guadalupe flood, but Town Creek flood wrecked the interior again
articles.summary: "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged."
articles.body:
Rebuilding after one flood is difficult enough. At Texas' Riverside Nature Center, staff restored the historic Lawson Store after a 2025 flood linked to backflow from the Guadalupe River, only to see a 2026 flood rip through the interior all over again.

The Kerr County Lead reported that the floods were very different, according to Riverside Nature Center's executive director Becky Etzler. The 2025 event followed the more familiar pattern of Guadalupe River backflow, but the 2026 flooding came out of Town Creek, which she described as a "rampaging monster."

Although the structure remained intact, the interior work completed after the first disaster did not. "All of the new renovations from 2025 were damaged," Etzler said. "We had to virtually start again in the Lawson Store."

Riverside Nature Center began in 1994 under founder Susan Sander, a Wisconsin-born freelance photographer. Through volunteer effort and privately raised funds, the organization acquired three historic homesteads and developed them into a regional natural resource hub.

Staff naturalist China Rubiano now oversees surveys of birds, butterflies, and plants, monitors seasonal changes in native species, and cares for Shucks — the center's captive-bred corn snake.

A large shipping container being used for storage after the first flood broke loose from its foundation, drifted across the parking lot, and crashed into the children's music garden, damaging several instruments.

Yet when it came to a stop, the container was positioned to shield the center's new 20,000-gallon rainwater-harvesting tank, which The Kerr County Lead reported was miraculously left undamaged.

When floodwaters damage community spaces, they can interrupt children's programs, create public health concerns through contaminated water and debris, strain local budgets with repeated repairs, and destabilize organizations families rely on for education and safe gathering spaces.

Rebuilding once is expensive, but rebuilding twice can drain time, money, and momentum from nonprofits, workers, and communities already struggling to recover.

Despite repeated damage, Riverside Nature Center has kept its programs going. According to The Kerr County Lead , Sprouts preschool nature classes grew from five families to more than 30 children, and Riverside Rangers and Wildflower Bunch seed-collection walks are still happening.

The center is adding help as it rebuilds. Former Schreiner University intern Bryley Torres joined the staff as the membership and marketing coordinator to support outreach efforts. Looking further ahead, Etzler hopes to expand the visitor center, continue building out the Nature Lab, and one day open an outdoor nature school.

The center is also maintaining its education schedule. A free talk was held on Aug. 19 with Kerr County AgriLife Extension Agent Sam Womble to discuss the New World screwworm and its risks to livestock, ranching, and pets.

articles.title: Another witness ordered released after a fatal shooting by a federal immigration agent in Texas
articles.summary: A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention....
articles.body:
A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention.

Daniel Tirado Pantoja was one of three passengers riding in a work van when the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who ran a homebuilding business, was shot July 7. The Department of Homeland Security has said Salgado Araujo, who had lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, had "weaponized his vehicle" and that the officer fired on him in self-defense.

U.S. District Judge Alfred Bennett in Houston ordered Tirado Pantoja released after finding that he had no criminal record and was neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community, according to court records.

"We're very glad that Mr. Tirado is going to be reunited with his family," said Ross Miller, an attorney for Tirado Pantoja.

Tirado Pantoja and another passenger, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego , have disputed accounts given by DHS about the confrontation with agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

They said the agents were never in front of the ICE vehicle and that Salgado Araujo had put vehicle in park as the agents were shooting. Tirado Pantoja also has said the agents' vehicle hit them from behind and then again on the driver's side.

Rojas Pliego was already released from detention last month. DHS did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about the judge's ruling.

Victor Salgado, the brother of the man killed, was also in the van and remains in custody. He also has asked a judge to order his release.

Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo's son, had said in social media post after the shooting that his father was on his way to work, picking up his workers, when the shooting occurred. He said his father was a hardworking man and was in the process of getting a work permit.

articles.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
articles.summary: They work better than patches, gum or pills, the most up-to-date evidence suggests.
articles.body:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine , which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking.

In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show . Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.

The review of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws.

It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC.

One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals.

"Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."

The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.

The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape.

Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them.

Around two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health.

According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year.

Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke.

Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.

You can search online for your local service with your postcode.
